claims.text: A thin Al-rich interlayer can shift the dominant creep mechanism of a CoCrFeNi-based HEA multilayer from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
The Al-rich interlayer causes the creep-mechanism shift by modifying interface coherency.
Changes in interface coherency alter dislocation pathways.
The initial CoCrFeNi-based HEA multilayer has coherent interfaces.
The initial multilayer contains no partial Al-rich layer.
Varying the Al content of an interfacial layer alters lattice mismatch.
Increasing or otherwise varying lattice mismatch through the Al-containing layer reduces interface coherency.
Both diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep processes are relevant in the proposed intermediate-to-high temperature regimes.
Interface coherency between the Al-rich layer and surrounding HEA layers affects dislocation motion.
Interface coherency between the Al-rich layer and surrounding HEA layers affects diffusion pathways.
An Al-rich layer can drive a coherent-to-partially-coherent interface transition.
The transition to partially coherent interfaces favors dislocation motion over long-range diffusion.
Disrupting interface coherency will reduce diffusion-mediated creep activity.
Disrupting interface coherency will increase dislocation-mediated creep activity.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition will produce a lower creep activation energy.
The proposed creep-mechanism transition will change the stress exponent.
Diffusion-mediated creep is dominant in a fully coherent CoCrFeNi-based multilayer without an Al-rich interlayer under the proposed test conditions.
The mechanism transition depends on Al concentration, interlayer thickness, temperature, and stress.
Outside suitable composition and testing ranges, creep may remain or revert to diffusion-mediated behavior if interface coherency is retained.
